headline: Bay Water Pushes Past 78, and the Fluke Follow It Straight to the Inlet
subhead: Weakfish wake up at the sedges on calm evenings, snapper blues crowd the creeks, and the stripers have gone strictly nocturnal.
body_markdown:
Back in the late eighties I mated for a captain out of Point Pleasant named Whitey Corson, and every July when the bay water got thick and warm he'd cut the engine off Tices Shoal, hand me the thermometer on a string, and say, 'Gus, when she reads high seventies, the game changes — you don't fight it, you follow it.' I've dropped that same thermometer a thousand times since, and this week it's telling the same old story it always does in the third week of July: the bay's running warm, the fish know it before we do, and if you want to catch anything worth keeping you fish where the water still has some snap to it.

Right now Barnegat Bay proper is sitting in the high 70s from Toms River down through Double Creek Channel, and that's pushed the fluke bite exactly where I told you it would a week back — out of the mid-bay flats and toward the inlet mouth and the ocean-side structure where the water still moves and stays a few degrees cooler. Double Creek Channel is still holding fish, don't get me wrong, but they're bunched tight along the deeper bends near the channel markers, not spread out over the flats like they were in June. Drifting the outgoing tide with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, right down in that 8 to 12 foot cut, has been putting keepers in the boat — nothing giant, mostly 17 to 19 inches with the occasional 4 or 5 pounder mixed in, but steady if you work the drift slow and keep that bucktail ticking bottom. The better numbers, though, are showing up right at the mouth of Barnegat Inlet and out on the ocean structure past the rocks, where boats working white and chartreuse Gulp on the drift, or bouncing squid strips over the reef structure, are finding a heavier grade of fish. That's the pattern I flagged last week and it's holding — fluke shifting off the warm back bay flats and into the inlet mouths as the water keeps climbing. I don't expect that to reverse itself before September.

Weakfish are the pleasant surprise. I wasn't optimistic a couple weeks back with the bay running so warm, but on the calm, flat evenings — and we've had a few — the sedges along Tices Shoal and down toward Barnegat Light have been holding fish right at last light. Small chartreuse Bass Assassins on a light jighead, or a live spearing under a popping cork fished slow along the grass edges on the last of the incoming tide, has been the ticket. Nothing over three pounds that I've heard of, but a legal weakfish in this bay in mid-July is nothing to complain about, and it lines up with what we expected — the bite rebuilding on those quiet, warm nights when the water lays flat and the bait gets nervous along the marsh edges.

Striped bass have gone strictly nighttime on us, and that's just thermal common sense — nobody wants to burn energy chasing bait in 78-degree water during the day when they can slide into the current breaks after dark and feed when it's cooler. The rocks at Barnegat Light and the deeper rips right at the inlet are your best bet after sundown, working bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig or swimming a Bomber-style plug through the current seam on the last two hours of the outgoing. I had a report of a couple of schoolies and one fish pushing 30 inches taken that way earlier this week, fished right at the change of tide around midnight. If you want stripers right now, you're setting your alarm, not your watch.

Snapper blues are thick in the back creeks — Forked River, Cedar Creek, the mouth of Double Creek — and that's about as reliable a July signal as we get on this bay. Where you've got snappers stacked up chasing spearing along the docks, the adult bluefish and the bigger bait schools generally aren't far behind. We haven't seen the blitz conditions here yet that they're getting up around Belmar with those bunker schools working the surf, but given how consistent that pattern's been building along the coast, I wouldn't be shocked if it starts creeping south toward Island Beach and the Barnegat surf in the next week or two. Worth keeping an eye on the beach at IBSP in the early morning hours — bluefish under working bunker schools can show up fast and disappear just as quick.

Blowfish are doing what blowfish do this time of year — steady, unglamorous, and dependable on the bay bottom in 6 to 10 feet around Double Creek and the flats off Waretown, squid strips or a small piece of clam on a hi-lo rig. Kingfish are scattered but present on the ocean side and right in the surf at Island Beach on bloodworms and sandworm, best on the last of the incoming over clean sand.

Looking ahead, we're sliding toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which should ease the tidal push a touch and favor slower presentations in the rips and at the inlet mouth — good news for fluke guys working bucktails and good news for anyone soaking bunker chunks for stripers after dark. If this stable, calm weather holds, I expect this whole pattern — fluke pushing to the inlet, weakfish working the sedges at dusk, bass strictly nocturnal — to hold through the end of the month. That's about as safe a bet as you get on this bay in the height of summer.
